title: Chapter 29. Of Those Things That Weaken, or Tend to the Dissolution of a Commonwealth
paragraphs: Though nothing that mortals make can be immortal, yet if men had the use of reason they pretend to, their commonwealths might be secured, at least, from perishing by internal diseases. For by the nature of their institution they are designed to live as long as mankind, or as the laws of nature, or as justice itself, which gives them life. So when they come to be dissolved, not by external violence but by internal disorder, the fault is not in men as they are the matter, but as they are the makers and orderers of them. For men, when at last they grow weary of irregular jostling and hewing one another, and desire with all their hearts to conform themselves into one firm and lasting edifice, are nevertheless unable — for want both of the art of making fit laws to square their actions by, and of the humility and patience to suffer the rude and cumbersome points of their present greatness to be planed off — to be assembled, without the help of a very able architect, into anything but a crazy building, which can hardly last out their own time and must inevitably fall on the heads of their posterity.

Among the infirmities of a commonwealth, then, I will reckon in the first place those that arise from an imperfect institution, and resemble the diseases of a natural body which proceed from a defective procreation.

Of which this is one: 'That a man to obtain a kingdom is sometimes content with less power than is necessarily required for the peace and defence of the commonwealth.' From this it follows that when the power thus set aside has, for public safety, to be resumed, the resumption has the look of an unjust act — which disposes great numbers of men, when occasion is presented, to rebel; just as the bodies of children begotten by diseased parents are subject either to untimely death or to purging the ill quality derived from their vicious conception by breaking out into boils and scabs. When kings deny themselves some such necessary power, it is not always (though sometimes) out of ignorance of what is necessary to the office they undertake, but often out of a hope to recover the same again at their pleasure. In which they do not reason well; for those who hold them to their promises shall be backed against them by foreign commonwealths, which, for the good of their own subjects, let slip few occasions to weaken the estate of their neighbours. So Thomas Becket, archbishop of Canterbury, was supported against Henry the Second by the pope — the subjection of churchmen to the commonwealth having been dispensed with by William the Conqueror at his accession, when he took an oath not to infringe the liberty of the Church. So too the barons, whose power had been raised by William Rufus (to gain their help in transferring the succession from his elder brother to himself) to a degree inconsistent with the sovereign power, were upheld in their rebellion against King John by the French. Nor does this happen in monarchy alone. For whereas the style of the ancient Roman commonwealth was 'the Senate and people of Rome,' neither the Senate nor the people claimed the whole power; and this first caused the seditions of Tiberius Gracchus, Gaius Gracchus, Lucius Saturninus, and others; and afterwards the wars between the Senate and the people, under Marius and Sulla, and again under Pompey and Caesar, leading to the extinction of their democracy and the setting up of monarchy.

The people of Athens bound themselves from one action only — that no man, on pain of death, should propose the renewing of the war for the island of Salamis; and yet even by that, if Solon had not caused it to be given out that he was mad, and afterwards, in the gesture and dress of a madman, proposed it in verse to the people who flocked around him, they would have had an enemy perpetually in readiness at the very gates of their city. Such are the damages, or evasions, that all commonwealths are reduced to whose power is even slightly limited.

In the second place, I take notice of the diseases of a commonwealth that proceed from the poison of seditious doctrines, of which one is: 'That every private man is judge of good and evil actions.' This is true in the condition of mere nature, where there are no civil laws; and also under civil government, in such cases as are not determined by the law. But otherwise, it is plain that the measure of good and evil actions is the civil law, and the judge is the legislator, who is always the representative of the commonwealth. From this false doctrine, men are disposed to debate with themselves, and to dispute the commands of the commonwealth, and afterwards to obey or disobey them as in their private judgement they shall think fit; by which the commonwealth is distracted and weakened.

Another doctrine repugnant to civil society is that 'whatever a man does against his conscience is sin' — and it depends on the presumption of making oneself judge of good and evil. For a man's conscience and his judgement are the same thing; and as the judgement, so also the conscience may be erroneous. So though the man who is subject to no civil law sins in all he does against his conscience (because he has no other rule to follow but his own reason), it is not so for the man who lives in a commonwealth, because the law is the public conscience, by which he has already undertaken to be guided. Otherwise, given the diversity that there is of private consciences, which are only private opinions, the commonwealth must inevitably be distracted, and no man would dare to obey the sovereign power any further than it shall seem good in his own eyes.

It has also been commonly taught 'that faith and sanctity are not to be attained by study and reason, but by supernatural inspiration, or infusion.' Granted that, I do not see why any man should give a reason for his faith, or why every Christian should not also be a prophet, or why any man should take the law of his country, rather than his own inspiration, as the rule of his action. And so we fall again into the fault of taking upon ourselves to judge of good and evil, or of making such private men as claim to be supernaturally inspired into judges of it — to the dissolution of all civil government. Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by those accidents that bring us into the presence of those who speak to us; and these accidents are all contrived by God Almighty, and yet are not supernatural, but only — because of the great number of them concurring in every effect — unobservable. Faith and sanctity are indeed not very frequent, but they are not miracles; they are brought about by education, discipline, correction, and other natural ways, by which God works them in his elect at such time as he thinks fit. And these three opinions, harmful to peace and to government, have in this part of the world proceeded chiefly from the tongues and pens of unlearned divines, who, joining the words of Holy Scripture together other than as agrees with reason, do what they can to make men think that sanctity and natural reason cannot stand together.

A fourth opinion, repugnant to the nature of a commonwealth, is this: 'That the holder of the sovereign power is subject to the civil laws.' It is true that sovereigns are all subject to the laws of nature, because those laws are divine and cannot be abrogated by any man or commonwealth. But to those laws which the sovereign himself — that is, which the commonwealth — makes, he is not subject. For to be subject to the laws is to be subject to the commonwealth, that is, to the sovereign representative — that is, to himself; which is not subjection but freedom from the laws. This error, because it sets the laws above the sovereign, also sets a judge above him, and a power to punish him — which is to make a new sovereign; and again, for the same reason, a third, to punish the second; and so on without end, to the confusion and dissolution of the commonwealth.

A fifth doctrine that tends to the dissolution of a commonwealth is that 'every private man has an absolute property in his goods, such as excludes the right of the sovereign.' Every man indeed has a property that excludes the right of every other subject; and he has it only from the sovereign power, without whose protection every other man would have an equal right to the same. But if the right of the sovereign is also excluded, he cannot perform the office they have put him into — which is to defend them both from foreign enemies and from the injuries of one another — and consequently there is no longer a commonwealth.

And if the property of subjects does not exclude the right of the sovereign representative to their goods, much less to their offices of judicature or execution, in which they represent the sovereign himself.

There is a sixth doctrine, plainly and directly against the essence of a commonwealth, and it is this: 'That the sovereign power may be divided.' For what is it to divide the power of a commonwealth, but to dissolve it? — for powers divided mutually destroy each other. And for these doctrines, men are chiefly beholden to some of those who, professing the laws, endeavour to make them depend on their own learning, and not on the legislative power.

And as false doctrine, so also often the example of a different form of government in a neighbouring nation disposes men to alter the form already settled. So the people of the Jews were stirred up to reject God, and to call on the prophet Samuel for a king after the manner of the nations. So also the lesser cities of Greece were continually disturbed with seditions of the aristocratic and democratic factions; one part of almost every commonwealth desiring to imitate the Lacedaemonians, the other the Athenians. And I do not doubt that many men were content to see the late troubles in England out of an imitation of the Low Countries, supposing that to grow rich no more was needed than to change, as they had done, the form of government. For the constitution of human nature is of itself subject to a desire for novelty; and when men are prodded toward that by the neighbourhood of those who have been enriched by it, it is almost impossible for them not to be content with those who urge them to change, and to love the first beginnings, even though they are aggrieved by the continuance of the disorder — like hot-blooded men who, having got the itch, tear themselves with their own nails until they can endure the smart no longer.

And as for rebellion in particular against monarchy: one of its most frequent causes is the reading of the books of politics and histories of the ancient Greeks and Romans; from which young men, and all others unprovided with the antidote of solid reason, receiving a strong and delightful impression of the great exploits of war achieved by the leaders of their armies, also receive a pleasing idea of all those leaders did besides — and imagine that their great prosperity proceeded, not from the rivalry of particular men, but from the virtue of their popular form of government; not considering the frequent seditions and civil wars produced by the imperfection of their politics. From the reading, I say, of such books, men have undertaken to kill their kings, because the Greek and Latin writers in their books and discussions of politics make it lawful, and laudable, for any man to do so, provided that before doing it he calls the king a tyrant. For they do not say regicide — that is, the killing of a king — but tyrannicide, the killing of a tyrant, is lawful. From the same books, those who live under a monarch take up the opinion that the subjects in a popular commonwealth enjoy liberty, but that in a monarchy they are all slaves. I say it is those who live under a monarchy who take up such an opinion, not those who live under a popular government — for they find no such thing. In short, I cannot imagine how anything can be more prejudicial to a monarchy than allowing such books to be publicly read without immediately applying such correctives as discreet teachers can fit to take away their venom; a venom I will not hesitate to compare to the bite of a mad dog — a disease the physicians call hydrophobia, or fear of water. For as the man so bitten has a continual torment of thirst, and yet abhors water, and is in such a state as if the poison were trying to turn him into a dog, so when a monarchy has once been bitten to the quick by those democratical writers who continually snarl at that estate, it wants nothing more than a strong monarch — yet, when it has him, out of a certain tyrannophobia, a fear of being strongly governed, it abhors him.

As there have been doctors who hold that there are three souls in a man, so also there are those who think that there may be more souls (that is, more sovereigns) than one in a commonwealth; and they set up a supremacy against the sovereignty, canons against laws, and a ghostly authority against the civil, working on men's minds with words and distinctions that in themselves signify nothing, but betray (by their obscurity) that there walks (as some think invisibly) another kingdom — a kind of kingdom of fairies in the dark. Now since it is plain that the civil power and the power of the commonwealth are the same thing, and that supremacy, and the power of making canons and granting faculties, implies a commonwealth, it follows that where one is sovereign and another supreme, where one can make laws and another make canons, there must be two commonwealths over one and the same subjects, which is a kingdom divided in itself and cannot stand. For notwithstanding the insignificant distinction between 'temporal' and 'ghostly,' they are still two kingdoms, and every subject is subject to two masters. For seeing the ghostly power claims the right to declare what is sin, it claims by consequence the right to declare what is law (sin being nothing but the transgression of the law); and again, the civil power claiming to declare what is law, every subject must obey two masters, who will both have their commands observed as law — which is impossible. Or, if it is only one kingdom, either the civil (which is the power of the commonwealth) must be subordinate to the ghostly, or the ghostly subordinate to the temporal — and then there is no supremacy but the temporal. So when these two powers oppose one another, the commonwealth cannot but be in great danger of civil war and dissolution. For the civil authority, being more visible and standing in the clearer light of natural reason, cannot but draw to it at all times a very considerable part of the people; and the spiritual, though it stands in the darkness of school distinctions and hard words, yet, because the fear of darkness and ghosts is greater than other fears, cannot lack a party sufficient to trouble, and sometimes to destroy, a commonwealth. And this is a disease which not unfitly may be compared to the epilepsy, or falling-sickness (which the Jews took to be one kind of possession by spirits), in the natural body. For as in this disease there is an unnatural spirit, or wind, in the head, which obstructs the roots of the nerves and, moving them violently, takes away the motion they should naturally have from the power of the soul in the brain, and so causes violent and irregular motions (which men call convulsions) in the parts, so that a man seized with it falls down sometimes into the water and sometimes into the fire, as one deprived of his senses; so also in the body politic, when the spiritual power moves the members of a commonwealth by the terror of punishments and the hope of rewards (which are its nerves) otherwise than by the civil power (which is the soul of the commonwealth) they ought to be moved, and by strange and hard words suffocates the people, it either overwhelms the commonwealth with oppression, or casts it into the fire of a civil war.

Sometimes also in the merely civil government there is more than one soul: as when the power of levying money (which is the nutritive faculty) has depended on a general assembly; the power of conduct and command (which is the motive faculty) on one man; and the power of making laws (which is the rational faculty) on the accidental consent not only of those two but also of a third. This endangers the commonwealth, sometimes for want of consent to good laws, but most often for want of such nourishment as is necessary to life and motion. For though few perceive that such a government is not government, but a dividing of the commonwealth into three factions, and call it 'mixed monarchy,' the truth is that it is not one independent commonwealth but three independent factions; not one representative person but three. In the kingdom of God there may be three persons independent without breach of unity in God who reigns; but where men reign, who are subject to diversity of opinions, it cannot be so. And so if the king bears the person of the people, and the general assembly bears also the person of the people, and another assembly bears the person of a part of the people, they are not one person, nor one sovereign, but three persons and three sovereigns.

To what disease in the natural body of man I might exactly compare this irregularity of a commonwealth, I do not know. But I have seen a man who had another man growing out of his side, with a head, arms, breast, and stomach of his own: if he had had another man growing out of his other side too, the comparison might then have been exact.

So far I have named such diseases of a commonwealth as are of the greatest and most present danger. There are others, not so great, which are nevertheless not unfit to be noted. First, the difficulty of raising money for the necessary uses of the commonwealth, especially in the approach of war. This difficulty arises from the opinion every subject has of a property in his lands and goods exclusive of the sovereign's right to the use of the same. From this it follows that the sovereign power, which foresees the necessities and dangers of the commonwealth, finding the passage of money to the public treasure obstructed by the tenacity of the people — whereas it ought to extend itself, to meet and prevent such dangers in their beginnings — contracts itself as long as it can, and when it can no longer, struggles with the people by stratagems of law to obtain little sums; and when those will not suffice, is forced at last violently to open the way for present supply, or to perish. And being often put to these extremities, it at last reduces the people to their due temper — or else the commonwealth must perish. So we may compare this distemper very aptly to an ague, in which the fleshy parts, being congealed or by venomous matter obstructed, leave the veins which by their natural course empty themselves into the heart unsupplied (as they ought to be) from the arteries; whereby there first comes a cold contraction and trembling of the limbs, and afterwards a hot and strong endeavour of the heart to force a passage for the blood; and before it can do that, it contents itself with the small refreshment of such things as cool for a time, till (if nature is strong enough) it at last breaks the contumacy of the parts obstructed, and disperses the venom in sweat; or (if nature is too weak) the patient dies.

Again, there is sometimes in a commonwealth a disease which resembles pleurisy: namely, when the treasure of the commonwealth, flowing out of its due course, is gathered together in too much abundance in one, or a few, private men, by monopolies or by the farming of the public revenues — just as the blood in pleurisy, getting into the membrane of the breast, breeds there an inflammation, accompanied with a fever and painful stitches.

Also, the popularity of a powerful subject (unless the commonwealth has very good security of his fidelity) is a dangerous disease; because the people, who should receive their motion from the authority of the sovereign, are drawn away by the flattery and the reputation of an ambitious man from their obedience to the laws, to follow a man whose virtues and designs they have no knowledge of. And this is commonly more dangerous in a popular government than in a monarchy, since they can easily be made to believe that they are the people. By this means it was that Julius Caesar, who was set up by the people against the Senate, having won to himself the affections of his army, made himself master of both the Senate and the people. And this proceeding of popular and ambitious men is plain rebellion, and may be likened to the effects of witchcraft.

Another infirmity of a commonwealth is the immoderate greatness of a town, when it is able to furnish out of its own precincts the number and expense of a great army; as also the great number of corporations, which are, as it were, many lesser commonwealths in the bowels of a greater, like worms in the entrails of a natural man.

To which may be added the liberty of disputing against absolute power, by pretenders to political prudence — who, though for the most part bred in the dregs of the people, yet, animated by false doctrines, are perpetually meddling with the fundamental laws, to the vexation of the commonwealth, like the little worms which physicians call ascarides.

We may further add the insatiable appetite, or bulimia, of enlarging dominion, with the incurable wounds often received from the enemy in pursuit of it; and the wens of unannexed conquests, which are many times a burden, and with less danger lost than kept; and likewise the lethargy of ease, and the consumption of riotous and vain expense.

Lastly, when in a war (foreign or internal) the enemies have won a final victory — so that the forces of the commonwealth, keeping the field no longer, can no longer protect their subjects in their loyalty — then is the commonwealth DISSOLVED, and every man at liberty to protect himself by such courses as his own discretion shall suggest. For the sovereign is the public soul, giving life and motion to the commonwealth; which once expiring, the members are no more governed by it than the carcase of a man is governed by his departed (though immortal) soul. For though the right of a sovereign monarch cannot be extinguished by the act of another, the obligation of the members may be. For he who wants protection may seek it anywhere; and when he has it, he is obliged (without any fraudulent pretence of having submitted himself out of fear) to protect his protection as long as he is able. But when the power of an assembly is once suppressed, the right of the same perishes utterly, because the assembly itself is extinct; and consequently there is no possibility for the sovereignty to re-enter.
